artiest/kevin-saunderson.text:
Kevin Saunderson is an American DJ and producer and one of the creators of techno. He was born in 1964 in Brooklyn, New York, and as a child moved to Belleville, a town near Detroit. At high school he became friends with Juan Atkins and Derrick May. The three listened to Kraftwerk and to the radio DJ The Electrifying Mojo, and were later called the Belleville Three. Saunderson first studied telecommunications, but saw his friends making records and wanted to do the same. With Atkins's help he made Triangle of Love in 1986, under the name Kreem. A year later he started his own label, KMS.

His greatest success came almost by accident. In 1987 he recorded an instrumental track at home and looked for a singer to go with it. Paris Grey wrote a lyric and so Big Fun came about. The song was released in 1988 under the name Inner City and became a worldwide hit, as did its follow-up Good Life. Inner City joined the hard machine rhythms of Detroit to house, disco and soul and so made techno suitable for the charts.

Under other names Saunderson continued to make rougher work. As Reese he released Just Want Another Chance in 1988. Its deep, growling bass line, made on a Casio CZ-1000, later became a building block of jungle and drum and bass. With the project E-Dancer he made more underground techno, such as the 1998 album Heavenly. In this way he has one foot in the clubs and the other in the hit parade.
artiest/kevin-saunderson.listen: Listen to Big Fun by Inner City. Notice how the tight electronic drums and bass from Detroit go together with Paris Grey's soulful vocals.

artiest/khaled.text:
Khaled was born in 1960 in Oran, in what was then French Algeria. As a teenager he began recording under the name Cheb Khaled, Arabic for the young Khaled, in the genre raï, a popular style from the Maghreb. In 1985 he was proclaimed king of raï in Oran. A year later the first raï festival in France was organised in Bobigny near Paris, and Khaled got the chance to record in France. The 1988 album Kutché, made with the Algerian jazz musician Safy Boutella, brought him to attention in France. He settled there.

In 1992 he dropped the prefix Cheb and recorded the album Khaled, produced by Don Was. The single Didi became a big hit in Europe, the Arab world and parts of Asia. Later came Aïcha, which Jean-Jacques Goldman wrote for him, and the 2012 album C'est la vie, among others. Khaled sings in Arabic and French and brings traditional Algerian singing together with Western rhythms and styles, such as soul, rock and reggae.

His significance lies in the bridge he built between the Maghreb and Western audiences. He is regarded as a pioneer of world music and as one of the best-known African singers in the world. In this way he shows that a local folk music can break through worldwide.
artiest/khaled.listen: Listen to Didi and notice how the Arabic singing and the rhythms and sound of the Western production together form a single song. Try to hear which elements come from the Maghreb and which from pop music.

artiest/ki-nartosabdho.text: Ki Nartosabdho, born Sunarto, was a dalang, a puppeteer of the Javanese shadow play wayang kulit, and an extremely prolific composer. He began in 1945 as a drummer with a theatre troupe in Semarang and learned puppetry by watching closely. A radio broadcast in 1958 made him known throughout Indonesia. He wrote hundreds of gending, pieces for gamelan, in a lively Semarang style.
artiest/ki-nartosabdho.listen: Listen to Goyang Semarang: hear how the gongs divide the piece into fixed cycles, while the voice and drum move playfully through them.

artiest/kid-baltan.text:
Kid Baltan is the pseudonym of Dick Raaijmakers, a Dutch composer, theatre maker and theorist, born in 1930 in Maastricht and died in 2013 in The Hague. The name is Dik NatLab backwards, a reference to his nickname and to the Philips Natuurkundig Laboratorium (Physics Laboratory). He studied piano at the Royal Conservatoire in The Hague and from 1954 to 1960 worked at Philips in Eindhoven on electro-acoustic research.

At Philips he formed the duo Electrosoniks with Tom Dissevelt. Together they made some of the first electronic pop music. Their most important album is The Fascinating World of Electronic Music, which appeared in the Netherlands in 1959. With electronic means he also made three experiments with popular music, which were later collected under the title Popular Electronics, with early Dutch electronic music from the Philips laboratories. Song of the Second Moon (1968) contains other work under his name.

After his time at Philips he worked at Utrecht University from 1960 to 1962. From 1963 to 1966 he had his own electronic music studio in The Hague with Jan Boerman. He was a co-founder of STEIM, the Studio for Electro-Instrumental Music. In 1966 he founded the electronic music studio at the Royal Conservatoire and taught there until 1995. He was regarded as a pioneer of electronic music and tape music, and also made a great deal of music theatre and theoretical publications. His archive is preserved at the Nederlands Muziek Instituut.
artiest/kid-baltan.listen: Listen to a track from The Fascinating World of Electronic Music. Notice the floating, whistling sounds from the studio and the rhythms that sound like pop, but without ordinary instruments.

artiest/kid-ory.text: Edward 'Kid' Ory led one of the most popular bands in New Orleans, in which King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, among others, played. He developed the tailgate style on the trombone: sliding tones and rhythmic counter-voices beneath the melody. In 1919 he moved to California and in 1922 his band in Los Angeles made one of the first recordings by Black New Orleans musicians. In Chicago he played on Armstrong's Hot Five records; his piece Muskrat Ramble became a classic. In the 1930s he gave up music for a while, but during the New Orleans revival of the 1940s he came back with a Creole Jazz Band of his own.
artiest/kid-ory.listen: Follow the trombone: sliding tones that fill the space beneath the trumpet.

artiest/kim-deal.text:
Kim Deal is an American singer and rock musician, born in 1961 in Dayton, Ohio. She grew up with hard rock such as AC/DC and Led Zeppelin and as a teenager formed a folk-rock band with her twin sister Kelley. She kept writing, sometimes a hundred songs in a few years. She studied at seven different colleges but never finished any of them, and worked in a hospital laboratory before music took hold of her.

In January 1986 she joined the Pixies, as bassist and second voice, under the name Mrs. John Murphy on Come on Pilgrim and Surfer Rosa. After Doolittle and a break she founded the Breeders, with Tanya Donelly of Throwing Muses, Josephine Wiggs and Britt Walford of Slint. The debut was Pod. Kelley then joined the band. In 1993 Last Splash went platinum, with the hit single Cannonball. In 1995, under the name Tammy Ampersand, she made the album Pacer with the Amps. Title TK (2002) and Mountain Battles (2008) followed later.

In 2004 she rejoined the Pixies and left the band in 2013 to concentrate on the Breeders. In 2018 the album All Nerve appeared, the first since Last Splash with the same line-up. In 2024 she released her first solo album, Nobody Loves You More. Deal is an important voice in alternative rock, as a woman in a band that influenced many other groups.
artiest/kim-deal.listen: Listen to Cannonball by the Breeders. Notice the thudding bass line, the almost whispered vocals and how the silence between the guitar strokes builds tension.

artiest/kim-kashkashian.text:
Kim Kashkashian is an American violist, born in 1952 in Detroit to Armenian American parents. Her father had a baritone voice and sang Armenian folk songs, which influenced her. She began violin at the age of eight and at twelve switched to the viola at the Interlochen Arts Academy. She then studied at the Peabody Conservatory in Baltimore, among other places. She has built her career in the United States and Europe and is regarded as one of the best violists in the world.

In the 1980s she was already recording works by Mozart and Schubert, such as the Divertimento K.563, the Kegelstatt Trio and a Schubert quartet. She also recorded a great deal of more recent music, including Shostakovich's viola sonata (1991) and the albums Elegies (1986) and Kammermusik no. 1-7 (1992). She worked with many great contemporary composers. In 2013 she won a Grammy for Best Classical Instrumental Solo.

Kashkashian taught in Philadelphia, New York and Bloomington. In 1989 she moved to Germany and became a teacher in Freiburg and later at the Hanns Eisler Hochschule in Berlin. In 2000 she returned to the United States and taught viola and chamber music at the New England Conservatory in Boston. In this way she contributed to the recognition of the viola as a solo instrument, with a warm, dark sound that inspires many composers.
artiest/kim-kashkashian.listen: Listen to Mozart's Divertimento K.563 in Kashkashian's recording. Notice the dark, warm tone of the viola among the other strings.

artiest/king-crimson.text:
King Crimson was an English rock band, founded in London in 1968 by guitarist Robert Fripp, drummer Michael Giles, bassist and singer Greg Lake, wind player and keyboardist Ian McDonald and lyricist Peter Sinfield. Fripp was the only member who stayed throughout its history. The band broke through in July 1969 as the support act for The Rolling Stones in Hyde Park. In October of that year In the Court of the Crimson King appeared, which is regarded as one of the cornerstones of progressive rock. The opening track 21st Century Schizoid Man was hard and distorted, while other tracks were bathed in the sound of the Mellotron.

The first line-up fell apart after only a year; Lake left for Emerson, Lake & Palmer. Fripp carried on with new musicians each time, on In the Wake of Poseidon (1970), Lizard (1970) and Islands (1971). From 1972 he worked with drummer Bill Bruford and bassist John Wetton, among others, and made the more experimental Larks' Tongues in Aspic (1973) and Red (1974). In the 1980s a new group came along with Adrian Belew and Tony Levin, which worked influences of new wave, minimal music and Indonesian gamelan into Discipline (1981).

King Crimson drew inspiration from classical music, jazz, folk and free improvisation, and liked to play in unusual time signatures. The music sounded more European than the blues rock of its contemporaries. The band had a great influence on Yes and Genesis, and later on alternative rock and metal. In 2021 King Crimson came to a definitive end.
artiest/king-crimson.listen: Listen to the title track In the Court of the Crimson King and notice the Mellotron: the choirs and strings you hear are recordings on tape, played back via a keyboard. Hear how that sound makes the song solemn and grand.

artiest/king-curtis.text:
King Curtis, born Curtis Montgomery and known as Curtis Ousley, was an American saxophonist who played rhythm and blues, jazz and rock 'n' roll. He was born in 1934 in Fort Worth, Texas, and after his adoption took the surname Ousley. At school he played with Ornette Coleman. He began saxophone at twelve and turned down university scholarships to play in Lionel Hampton's band. In 1952 he moved to New York and became a session musician. He played tenor, alto and soprano saxophone, and was also a bandleader, musical director and producer.

His solos and riffs appear on other people's hit singles, such as Yakety Yak by The Coasters (1958) and Respect by Aretha Franklin (1967). He himself scored with Soul Twist (1962) and Soul Serenade (1964), among others. In 1965 he switched to Atlantic Records and made Memphis Soul Stew and Ode to Billie Joe (both 1967). In 1966 he recorded three tracks with Jimi Hendrix, which were later lost in a fire in Atlantic's archive. He led the Kingpins, Aretha Franklin's backing band, who in 1965 played for the Beatles at Shea Stadium. His group included Richard Tee, Cornell Dupree, Jerry Jemmott and Bernard Purdie, among others.

His style was syncopated and percussive, versatile and powerful. He drew his inspiration from Lester Young, Louis Jordan and Illinois Jacquet. Curtis chose rhythm and blues because he found it the most beautiful and could make a good living from it. In this way he became the saxophone behind many soul records of his time. He died in 1971.
artiest/king-curtis.listen: Listen to Soul Serenade by King Curtis. Notice the broad, warm tone of the tenor saxophone and how the band lets the rhythm run on calmly.

artiest/king-jammy.text:
King Jammy, also known as Prince Jammy, is the stage name of Lloyd Woodrowe James, a Jamaican dub mixer, sound system owner and producer, born in 1947. In the late 1960s he earned money building amplifiers and repairing electrical equipment in his mother's house in Waterhouse, a district of Kingston. He then started a sound system of his own and built equipment for other systems. In the early 1970s he worked in Canada for a few years. In 1976 he returned to Kingston and set up a studio of his own in his in-laws' house.

His musical career began as a dub master in King Tubby's studio. When Philip Smart left for New York, Jammy took his place. His dubs are known for their clear sound and their use of effects. In the late 1970s he began releasing productions of his own, including Black Uhuru's debut album in 1977. In the 1980s he became one of the most influential producers of dancehall.

His biggest hit was Under Me Sleng Teng by Wayne Smith from 1985, with an entirely digital rhythm line. Many people call this song the first digital riddim in reggae, and with it the beginning of the modern dancehall era. Later Jammy digitised old riddims such as Real Rock and Far East. In this way he showed how dub could grow from King Tubby's studio into the electronic sound of dancehall.
artiest/king-jammy.listen: Listen to Under Me Sleng Teng by Wayne Smith. Notice the rhythm line that comes entirely from an electronic keyboard and how bare and tight the accompaniment sounds.

artiest/king-oliver.text: Joe 'King' Oliver was the most important cornetist of New Orleans in the 1910s. He was known for his playing with mutes, with which he could make the trumpet 'talk'. In 1918 he left for Chicago and from 1922 he led the Creole Jazz Band there at the Lincoln Gardens. He brought in the young Louis Armstrong as second cornetist; the two played breaks together that seemed to be invented on the spot. In 1923 the band recorded a series of records at Gennett and OKeh that are regarded as the most important documents of the New Orleans style. Oliver later suffered from gum trouble, lost his band and his money and died in poverty in Savannah, Georgia, in 1938.
artiest/king-oliver.listen: In Dipper Mouth Blues, listen to Oliver's muted solo: three choruses that took on a fixed form.

artiest/king-oliver-s-creole-jazz-band.text:
King Oliver was an American cornet player and bandleader, born in Louisiana and active in New Orleans. From 1908 to 1917 he played there in brass bands and dance orchestras, including in Storyville, the city's entertainment district. When Storyville closed, he moved to Chicago. There, from 1922, he played at Lincoln Gardens with his own group, King Oliver and his Creole Jazz Band.

In that band played Louis Armstrong on second cornet, Johnny Dodds on clarinet, Baby Dodds on drums, Lil Hardin on piano, Honoré Dutrey on trombone and Bill Johnson on bass. The recordings the group made in 1923, for Gennett, Okeh, Paramount and Columbia among others, let you hear the New Orleans style: collective improvisation, in which all the horns play their own line at the same time. Because recording was acoustic, into a horn, Armstrong, with his powerful sound, had to stand in the corner of the studio.

Oliver was also an innovator on his instrument. He used all kinds of mutes, such as the rubber plunger, and his solo in Dippermouth Blues is regarded as a well-known example. As a composer he wrote pieces that are still played, including Canal Street Blues and Doctor Jazz. Armstrong saw him as his great model. Oliver himself was dealt little money and health in the 1930s, and died in poverty in 1938.
artiest/king-oliver-s-creole-jazz-band.listen: Listen to Dipper Mouth Blues and notice the collective improvisation: try to follow the cornets and the clarinet separately. Can you also hear the solo with the mute?

artiest/king-tubby.text:
King Tubby's real name was Osbourne Ruddock. He was born in 1941 in Kingston, Jamaica, and began as a repairer of radios and televisions. In the late 1950s sound systems became popular, large sound installations with which DJs built outdoor parties. Tubby repaired their equipment, built large amplifiers and immersed himself in electronics and sound engineering. In 1968 he started his own sound system, Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi, which stood out for echo and reverb effects that until then could only be heard in a studio.

In that same year he went to work for the producer Duke Reid. He made versions of existing songs without vocals, over which the MCs of the sound systems could toast. He soon discovered that he could do much more with the faders and effects of the mixing desk. In 1971 he opened a studio of his own in Waterhouse. There he took instruments out and brought them back in, put echo and reverb on the drums and let the horns disappear into a thin squeal with a filter. In this way he played the mixing desk as an instrument. With Lee Perry he made Blackboard Jungle Dub (1973), one of the first dub albums. His best-known dub is King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown (1974), with Augustus Pablo on melodica.

Tubby did not record musicians himself. He worked with the tapes of other producers and made something new of them. For this reason he is often seen as the inventor of the remix, which later turned up everywhere in dance and electronic music. He also trained new engineers, such as King Jammy and Scientist. In 1989 he was shot dead near his home.
artiest/king-tubby.listen: Listen to King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown and notice how the drums and bass keep dropping out and coming back, with echo behind them. Hear how Augustus Pablo's melodica floats above while Tubby takes the song apart at the mixing desk.

artiest/kings-of-leon.text:
Kings of Leon consists of the brothers Caleb, Nathan and Jared Followill and their cousin Matthew Followill. Their father, Ivan Leon Followill, was a preacher in the United Pentecostal Church. For years the family travelled through the southern United States, where he preached in churches and tents. The band was formed in 1999 in Mount Juliet, near Nashville in Tennessee. The name refers to their grandfather Leon.

In 2002 Nathan and Caleb signed with RCA. The debut Youth & Young Manhood (2003) had a raw sound, with southern rock and garage rock. It caught on in England and Ireland, but not in America: there 100,000 copies were sold, against some 750,000 abroad. The breakthrough at home came with Only by the Night (2008). The album reached number 1 in England, number 4 in America and was the best-selling album of 2008 in Australia. Sex on Fire reached number 1 in England, Ireland and Australia. Use Somebody won three Grammys in 2010, including Record of the Year.

Kings of Leon began in the line of the southern rock of bands such as Lynyrd Skynyrd. The success of Sex on Fire showed that a guitar band could still top the charts in 2008, at a time when pop and hip hop set the tone. A year later Mumford & Sons brought folk to the same arena scale.
artiest/kings-of-leon.listen: The working title of Sex on Fire was Set Us on Fire; only after a joke by a sound engineer did the current title stick. Notice the high tempo, well over 150 beats per minute, and Caleb Followill's hoarse voice, which has to rise above the guitars.

artiest/kino.text:
Kino was a rock band from Leningrad, present-day Saint Petersburg, in the Soviet Union. The band revolved around singer, guitarist and songwriter Viktor Tsoi. The group was formed in 1981, and in the autumn of that year Kino became a member of the Leningrad Rock Club, one of the few places where rock bands in the Soviet Union were more or less officially allowed to perform.

Kino's music was cool and tight, with influences of new wave and post-punk from the West. Tsoi sang in a low, somewhat flat voice about loneliness, longing and city life. His lyrics were simple but touched a whole generation of young Soviet citizens. In the second half of the 1980s, when the rules relaxed under Gorbachev, Kino grew into one of the most popular bands in the country. The album Группа крови (1988) brought the breakthrough to a large audience, and Tsoi played the lead role in the film Igla.

In August 1990 Viktor Tsoi died in a car accident in Latvia. With that, Kino ceased to exist. His songs remained well known in Russia and the other former Soviet republics, and his song about the longing for change became a song sung at protests. Kino shows how rock behind the Iron Curtain found a voice of its own, independent of what the state wanted to hear.
artiest/kino.listen: Listen to Группа крови and notice the cool, tight accompaniment of guitar, bass and drums. Hear how Tsoi sings almost unmoved in his low voice, and how that very restrained tone gives the song its tension.

artiest/kippie-moeketsi.text:
Kippie Moeketsi, in full Jeremiah Morolong Moeketsi, was a South African jazz musician and alto saxophonist. He was born in 1925 into a musical family in Johannesburg and was the youngest of eleven brothers. Almost all of them played an instrument, and a sister worked as a nurse. His nickname comes from his mother, who called through the street to find him, as if he were a chicken. At twenty he began on clarinet, but soon switched to saxophone. His brother, the pianist Jacob Moeketsi, was a model.

His career began in shebeens, with his group Band in Blue. He played in several bands, including the Shantytown Sextet, the Harlem Swingsters and above all the Jazz Epistles, which made him, Abdullah Ibrahim, then still Dollar Brand, Jonas Gwangwa and Hugh Masekela known. He was sometimes called the father of South African jazz and the Charlie Parker of South Africa. Ibrahim wrote the composition Bra Joe from Kilimanjaro for him. He played in Todd Matshikiza's musical King Kong, which took him to London in 1961. After the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 most of his contemporaries went into exile, but he returned. Under the oppressive conditions he did not play for four years.

He can be heard on records such as Dollar Brand + 3 (1973) and Tshona! (1975). He died in 1983, destitute. His influence on Ibrahim, Masekela, Miriam Makeba and Gwangwa was great, and the jazz club Kippies in the Market Theatre in Johannesburg is named after him.
artiest/kippie-moeketsi.listen: Listen to Tshona! or to Dollar Brand + 3. Notice Moeketsi's alto, which rises above the rhythm section with a sharp, singing tone.

artiest/kishore-kumar.text:
Kishore Kumar, born Abhas Kumar Ganguly, was an Indian playback singer, musician and actor. He was born in 1929 in Khandwa, in what is now Madhya Pradesh, into a Bengali family. His father was a lawyer. His older brother Ashok became an actor in Hindi film, and later his brother Anoop followed. Kishore studied at the Christian College in Indore and died in 1987.

In Indian music he is regarded as one of the greatest and most influential singers. He was known for his yodelling and for his ability to sing songs in different voices. He sang in many genres and not only in Hindi, but also in Bengali, Marathi, Assamese, Gujarati, Kannada, Bhojpuri, Malayalam, Odia and Urdu. Besides film music, he released albums that were not connected to films, mainly in Bengali. Some of these are regarded as classics. His work ran from Kishore Sings For Kishore (1957) and Jhumroo (1961) to Love in Bombay (1974) and Adhikar (1985).

He won eight Filmfare Awards for best male playback singer, from twenty-eight nominations, and nobody has won or been nominated more often in that category. His brother Ashok said that his voice hits the microphone right at its most sensitive point. In 2013 he was chosen as the most popular male playback singer. An unreleased song of his fetched 15.6 lakh rupees at an auction in New Delhi in 2012.
artiest/kishore-kumar.listen: Listen to a film song by Kishore Kumar. Notice how he switches between soft singing, yodelling and funny little voices without losing the melody.

artiest/kiss.text:
Kiss was an American rock band from New York, formed in 1973 by Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons, who had previously played together in Wicked Lester. Drummer Peter Criss and guitarist Ace Frehley completed the line-up. The four took on the personas of comic-book characters: Starchild, Demon, Spaceman and Catman, each with its own face paint. Stanley came up with the name while they were driving through the city, and Frehley drew the logo with the two S's as lightning bolts.

The first records, Kiss, Hotter Than Hell and Dressed to Kill, sold moderately. The money ran out and the record company Casablanca was close to bankruptcy. The breakthrough came in 1975 with the live album Alive!, with a version of Rock and Roll All Nite that became the first top 40 hit. Destroyer followed in 1976, produced by Bob Ezrin with orchestra and choir, and the ballad Beth, which only gained popularity after being released as a B-side. The sound is straightforward hard rock with singalong choruses and hard guitars.

The audience came mainly for the show: Simmons spat fake blood and breathed fire, Frehley's guitar smoked and Criss's drum kit rose into the air. When sales declined in the early 1980s, the band took off the make-up in 1983, and the album Lick It Up brought a new generation of fans via MTV. In 1996 the original line-up returned with make-up, and in 2014 came induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2023 Kiss gave their last concert in New York. The band showed how important image and spectacle could become in rock history.
artiest/kiss.listen: Listen to Rock and Roll All Nite in the live version from Alive! and notice the audience, the guitar solo and the simple, loud chorus that is almost a singalong.

artiest/kitaro.text:
Kitaro's real name is Masanori Takahashi, and he was born in 1953 in Toyohashi, Japan, into a farming family. His parents wanted him to take an ordinary job, but he simply did not turn up and so convinced them that he had to make music. At high school he played electric guitar in a band that played rhythm and blues by Otis Redding and songs by The Beatles. In Tokyo he discovered the synthesizer, and he became keyboardist of the progressive rock band Far East Family Band.

In 1975 he met the German electronic musician Klaus Schulze, who produced two albums by the band and gave Kitaro tips for working with synthesizers. A year later Kitaro travelled through China, Laos, Thailand and India, and in 1977 he began a solo career. His great breakthrough came with the music for Silk Road, a documentary series by the Japanese broadcaster NHK that was broadcast from 1980. He made that music mainly with a Minimoog and Korg synthesizers, and demanded that the series be broadcast in stereo. The soundtracks sold millions of copies.

Kitaro's music is instrumental, calm and melodic, with long, floating sounds and influences from Asian music. He is regarded as one of the best-known names in new age. He won a Golden Globe for the film music of Heaven & Earth (1993) and a Grammy for the album Thinking of You. In this way Kitaro shows how the synthesizer can also express calm and space.
artiest/kitaro.listen: Listen to Theme from Silk Road and notice the soft, floating synthesizer sounds on which a simple melody slowly builds. Can you hear how the music conjures up images of a long journey through a wide landscape?

artiest/kitty-wells.text:
Kitty Wells was born Ellen Muriel Deason in Nashville in 1919. She sang as a child, learned guitar from her father and as a teenager performed with her sisters on local radio. At eighteen she married Johnnie Wright, who later became half of the duo Johnnie & Jack. Her stage name came from the folk ballad Sweet Kitty Wells. A first contract with RCA Victor produced no hits, and in 1950 she was dropped.

In 1952 she recorded It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels for Decca, in Owen Bradley's studio. The song was an answer to The Wild Side of Life by Hank Thompson and defended the woman in a world where all the blame was put on her. Some radio stations refused it, and the Grand Ole Opry briefly banned it, but the public wanted to hear it. It became the first number one on Billboard's country chart by a female singer. Later came Heartbreak U.S.A. in 1961, duets with Red Foley and Webb Pierce, and hits such as Making Believe, Amigo's Guitar and Password.

Her music is honky tonk, direct and unadorned, with a message in her songs that is often unusually sharp. She was the first female country singer with an LP of her own, in 1956, and in 1969 the first with her own television show. Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton continued her line with songs that attacked the same double standard. In 1976 came the Country Music Hall of Fame, in 1991 a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. She was called the Queen of Country Music.
artiest/kitty-wells.listen: Listen to It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels and notice the line in which she throws the blame back at the men, and how few instruments are needed to say it.

artiest/klaus-badelt.text: Klaus Badelt was born in 1967 in Frankfurt. In Germany he first wrote music for films and advertising. In 1998 Hans Zimmer asked him to come and work at Media Ventures in Santa Monica. There he worked on scores such as The Thin Red Line (1998) and Gladiator (2000). In 2002 he wrote The Time Machine, K-19: The Widowmaker and Equilibrium under his own name. For The Time Machine he received the World Soundtrack Award for Discovery of the Year in 2003. He became best known for Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl (2003). In the Filmmuziek Top 400 of NPO Klassiek, that music is listed under Zimmer and Badelt together. Later he wrote, among others, the Chinese film The Promise (2005) and Poseidon (2006).
artiest/klaus-badelt.listen: In Pirates of the Caribbean, notice the fast, dancing rhythm in the low strings and the horn themes above it, which are repeated in blocks again and again.

artiest/klaus-dinger.text:
Klaus Dinger was a German drummer, guitarist and songwriter. He was born in 1946 in Scherfede in Westphalia and grew up in Düsseldorf. After secondary school he trained as a carpenter and practised on pieces of wood until he could afford a drum kit. In 1966 he started the band The No, which drew inspiration from The Kinks and The Rolling Stones. He studied architecture for a while, but in the end chose music entirely. In the summer of 1970 Ralf Hütter asked him to drum on Kraftwerk's debut, and Dinger briefly became a member of the group.

In 1971 Dinger and guitarist Michael Rother left Kraftwerk and together started Neu!. With the producer Conny Plank they recorded the first album, Neu!, in Hamburg. On it Dinger played his famous beat for the first time: a tight, constantly repeated rhythm in four-four time with almost no interruptions. Later it was given the name motorik, although Dinger himself preferred to call it the long straight line. After Neu! 2 (1973), Dinger and Rother went their own ways. With his brother Thomas and Hans Lampe, Dinger founded La Düsseldorf, in which he played guitar and sang. Later he made solo records such as Néondian (1985). He died in 2008.

Dinger also had a clear idea of what a band should look like. He devised the name Neu! and the logo in the style of pop art, as a protest against consumer society. His motorik beat became one of the most recognisable sounds of krautrock and echoes through much later electronic music and indie rock.
artiest/klaus-dinger.listen: Listen to Hallogallo by Neu! and notice Klaus Dinger's drums: the same straight beat runs on for almost ten minutes, without rolls or breaks. Hear how Michael Rother's guitar floats above it and how that makes the song feel like a long drive on the motorway.

artiest/klaus-doldinger.text: Klaus Doldinger was born in 1936 in Berlin. At the Düsseldorf conservatoire he studied piano and later clarinet, then musicology. He became known as a jazz saxophonist. In 1971 he founded the band Passport, which was sometimes called the European counterpart of Weather Report. Besides saxophone he played keyboards and synthesizer. For television he wrote the theme music of the crime series Tatort in 1970, which is still used today. His music for Wolfgang Petersen's Das Boot (1981), about the crew of a German submarine, became known internationally. For Die unendliche Geschichte (1984) he wrote the score, together with Giorgio Moroder. Doldinger died in 2025.
artiest/klaus-doldinger.listen: In Das Boot, notice the heavy, pulsing synthesizer bass beneath a broad theme, and in Tatort the jazz saxophone above a tight rhythm.

artiest/klaus-meine.text:
Klaus Meine is a German singer, born in 1948 in Hanover. For decades he has been the frontman and main lyricist of the hard rock band Scorpions. The group had existed since 1965; Meine joined in 1969. Together with guitarist Rudolf Schenker he is the only member heard on all of the band's albums. As a boy he listened to Elvis Presley, Little Richard, Roy Orbison, The Everly Brothers, The Beatles and The Rolling Stones.

Meine has a high voice with a wide range. He wrote most of the Scorpions' lyrics. With drummer Herman Rarebell he wrote Rock You Like a Hurricane and Still Loving You, among others. In 1981, after a world tour and during the recording of the album Blackout, he lost his voice so badly that he could hardly speak. His doctor advised him to choose another profession. After therapy and two operations on his vocal cords he was able to sing again after all.

He wrote his best-known song alone: Wind of Change. The Scorpions played in Moscow in 1989, at the time when the Soviet Union was opening up to the West, and Meine was so impressed by the atmosphere that he made a song about it. After the fall of the Wall, Wind of Change became an anthem for the end of the Cold War. In 1990 Meine appeared with the Scorpions at the performance of Roger Waters's The Wall in Berlin. In this way a German hard rock singer became the voice of a historic moment.
artiest/klaus-meine.listen: Listen to Wind of Change and notice the beginning: a whistled melody above quiet guitar chords. Hear how Meine sings the verses softly and how the band only comes in with full force later.

artiest/klaus-nomi.text:
Klaus Nomi's real name was Klaus Sperber. He was born in 1944 in Immenstadt in Bavaria and grew up in the Ruhr area. As a boy he listened to opera, especially to Maria Callas, but he also bought records by Elvis Presley. In West Berlin he learned to sing as a baritone. He worked as a pastry chef and as an usher at the Deutsche Oper, where he sang arias for the staff after performances. In 1972 he left for New York.

There he attracted attention in 1978 during an evening at Irving Plaza. In a tight space suit with a transparent cape he sang an aria from Saint-Saëns's Samson et Dalila, after which he disappeared amid strobe light and smoke bombs. He then performed in clubs such as the Mudd Club and Max's Kansas City. With the songwriter Kristian Hoffman he put together a repertoire of his own songs such as Total Eclipse and the Nomi Song, and covers of pop songs from the 1960s, such as Lightnin' Strikes. In 1979 he was one of David Bowie's backing singers on Saturday Night Live. He made two albums, Klaus Nomi (1981) and Simple Man (1982).

Nomi combined opera, synthesizer pop and vaudeville. He sang in a high countertenor and wore heavy make-up, a plastic costume and a striking hairstyle. His performances made him a well-known figure in the art scene of the East Village. In 1983 he died of the effects of AIDS. He was one of the first well-known artists to die of the disease, at a time when even his friends did not dare to visit.
artiest/klaus-nomi.listen: Listen to The Cold Song, an aria from Henry Purcell's 1691 opera King Arthur. Notice how Nomi sings the old melody slowly and very high, and how strange and fragile that voice sounds in a pop performance.

artiest/klaus-schulze.text:
Klaus Schulze was a German composer and pioneer of electronic music. He was born in 1947 in Berlin. In 1969 he was the drummer of Tangerine Dream and played on their debut Electronic Meditation. A year later he founded Ash Ra Tempel with Manuel Göttsching. There too he left after one album, to go solo in 1971.

He made his first solo album Irrlicht (1972) without synthesizers, with an organ and a recording of an orchestra that was processed so that it became almost unrecognisable. The album is regarded as a milestone of early ambient. On Cyborg (1973) he used a synthesizer for the first time. Timewind (1975), full of references to Richard Wagner, and Moondawn (1976), his first album with a Moog, followed. With those records he became one of the founders of the Berlin School: long pieces in which repeated sequencer patterns change slowly. In the 1980s he began using digital instruments, and he produced Alphaville's The Breathtaking Blue (1989). He made more than sixty albums, also under the name Richard Wahnfried. He died in 2022.

Schulze sounded lighter and dreamier than Tangerine Dream, with occasional acoustic sounds such as a cello or an operatic voice. His music was appreciated by fans of new age, although he himself wanted nothing to do with that movement. Together with Tangerine Dream he laid the foundation for ambient and for much later electronic music.
artiest/klaus-schulze.listen: Listen to Bayreuth Return from Timewind, a piece of almost half an hour that fills a whole album side. Notice how the sounds change very slowly, without verse or chorus, so that you are in an atmosphere rather than listening to a song.

artiest/klein-orkest.text:
Klein Orkest was founded in The Hague in 1978 by singer and lyricist Harrie Jekkers and Koos Meinderts. The group came out of a failed cabaret programme, Het Groot Orkest, and at first played mainly at squat parties. Klein Orkest made kleinkunst (Dutch cabaret song) with a pop band: songs in which the lyrics are central, played with guitar, bass, drums and keyboards. In this way the group belongs to the line of Dutch chanson that later continues to Acda en de Munnik.

The regular line-up consisted of Jekkers, drummer Niek Nieuwenhuijsen, bassist Chris Prins and keyboardist Léon Smit. The first album Het leed versierd (1982) contained Laat mij maar alleen, which reached the Top 40. After the success of Doe Maar, Dutch-language bands were given more room on the radio. Over de muur was released on 1 November 1983, three days after the big demonstration against cruise missiles in The Hague. The song compares East and West Berlin and shows that both sides have their own form of unfreedom. In the summer of 1984 it became a hit; the album Later is al lang begonnen (1984) reached number 4. Roltrap naar de maan (1985) won an Edison.

In September 1985 Klein Orkest gave its last concert. Jekkers went back to the theatre and made solo records. After the fall of the Wall in 1989, Over de muur was released again, and since the first edition in 1999 the song has appeared every year in the Top 2000 of NPO Radio 2. From 2017 to 2019 the group toured the theatres once more.
artiest/klein-orkest.listen: Over de muur is built like a travel report: the verses describe streets and people on both sides of the Wall. Listen to how the chorus keeps returning to the birds flying over the wall, the only image that stays the same on both sides.

artiest/knut-buen.text:
Knut Buen is a Norwegian fiddler, composer, folklorist and publisher, born in 1948 in Kongsberg. He is the son of the folk musician Anders Buen and Margit Tjønn and the brother of Hauk Buen, Agnes Buen Garnås and the artist Kari Buen. He thus grew up in a family in which Norwegian folk music was a matter of course. In 1983 and 1986 he won the national music competition Landskappleiken.

Buen is known for his collection of traditional songs and melodies. With Hauk Buen he made the album Fykerud'n, with which he won a Spellemannprisen, the Norwegian music prize, in 1992. In 1994 a second prize followed for Bjølleslåtten, together with Kåre Nordstoga and Leif Rygg. He runs the publishing house Buen kulturverkstad and the record label Nyrenning, so that he collects, records and publishes the music himself. In 1999 he was appointed Knight First Class of the Order of St. Olav.

His own recordings include Stev og slått from 1996, Seljordsmarsjen from 2004 and Nordafjølls from 2012. The last of these contains folk songs and lydslåttar, dance melodies from the Norwegian region of Setesdal. Buen shows how alive that old music still is, and how a single fiddler can carry an entire tradition and pass it on to new listeners.
artiest/knut-buen.listen: Listen to Gangar etter Myllarguten. Notice the rhythm of the dance and how the fiddle plays the rhythm and the melody at the same time.

artiest/kodo.text:
Kodo is a professional taiko ensemble that has its home on the island of Sado in Japan. The group came into being in 1981 from the members of Ondekoza, a taiko group from 1971. Ondekoza's leader Den Tagayasu left just before the changeover and kept the old name. The leading player Eitetsu Hayashi left shortly after the founding to go solo, but did devise the new name. Kodo means heartbeat, the primal source of all rhythm, and can also be read as children of the drum. Mothers told how the music rocked their children to sleep.

The group made its debut in 1981 in the Berliner Philharmonie and in 1984 gave three sold-out concerts at the arts festival accompanying the Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Later the members built a village on Sado and started the annual festival Earth Celebration. Each year Kodo spends about a third of its time giving concerts in Japan, a third abroad and a third resting and preparing on the island. Its records include Ubu-Suna, Blessing of the Earth and Mondo Head.

The large taiko drums, the o-daiko, form the core of the sound, supplemented by flutes, the shamisen, dance and song. The repertoire consists of regional folk rhythms, pieces by contemporary composers and the members' own work. The strict training, once with running twice a day, is part of the reputation. Kodo brought taiko to audiences outside Japan and is regarded as one of the best-known and most respected taiko groups in the world.
artiest/kodo.listen: Listen to a piece for large taiko and notice how the drum can sound not only loud, but also soft and breathing, and how the players alternate with one another in the rhythms.

artiest/koichi-sugiyama.text: Koichi Sugiyama (1931–2021) first worked as a director in radio and television and wrote advertising music and pop songs. In his mid-fifties he began on game music. For Dragon Quest (1986) he wrote melodies in the style of Western classical music, with a solemn overture as the opening. He established a fixed pattern: a theme for the castle, the town, the field, the dungeon and the battles. Many later role-playing games adopted that pattern. Sugiyama had his game music played by orchestras early on and from 1987 organised concerts of game music. He wrote the music for the series until his death. He was also controversial for his nationalist political statements.
artiest/koichi-sugiyama.listen: Notice the classical form: a fanfare-like overture, clear melodies and harmonies that recall European Romanticism.

artiest/koji-kondo.text: Kōji Kondō (born in 1961) joined Nintendo in 1984. A year later he wrote the music for Super Mario Bros. (1985). The NES console had only a few sound channels: two for square waves, one for a triangle wave, one for noise and one for short samples. With those he had to make melody, bass and rhythm at the same time. The main theme has a Latin American rhythm and follows the tempo of Mario's jumps. For The Legend of Zelda (1986) he wrote a heroic march. In Ocarina of Time (1998) music itself became part of the game: the player plays melodies on an ocarina to open doors. His short, recognisable motifs became a model for game music.
artiest/koji-kondo.listen: Listen to how, with only three or four voices at a time, a complete melody, bass line and drum part sound.

artiest/komeda-quintet.text:
The Komeda Quintet was the group of the Polish pianist and composer Krzysztof Komeda, born Krzysztof Trzciński in 1931. He studied medicine, became an ear, nose and throat doctor and took his stage name to hide his jazz from colleagues at the clinic. With his Komeda Sextet he began playing modern jazz in the 1950s, at a time when jazz still had to fight for respect with the communist authorities. In this way he opened the way for jazz in Poland.

In the 1960s he toured Scandinavia, Germany and Eastern Europe and performed in Stockholm and Copenhagen. He wrote more than seventy film scores, including for Roman Polanski's films such as Nóż w wodzie (Knife in the Water), Cul-de-sac and Rosemary's Baby. His best-known record with the quintet is Astigmatic, which was recorded in 1965 and released in 1966. The music blends jazz with classical influences and Polish tradition and sounds lyrical, almost poetic.

Astigmatic is regarded as one of the most important European jazz albums. The critic Stuart Nicholson calls it a shift away from the American approach to a European aesthetic of its own. At the end of 1968 Komeda was injured in Los Angeles in a fall at a party, and he died in April 1969 at the age of 37. His influence is great: the Polish school of jazz came about partly through him, and since 1995 a jazz festival has borne his name.
artiest/komeda-quintet.listen: Listen to the title piece of Astigmatic and notice the calm, melodic line of the piano and the horns, which recalls European chamber music more than American swing.

artiest/kongar-ol-ondar.text: Kongar-ol Ondar grew up in the west of Tuva and became a master of khöömei, the throat singing in which one singer lets a fundamental and a whistling overtone be heard at the same time. In 1992 he won an international throat-singing competition, after which invitations from Europe and America followed. He invited the blind American blues musician Paul Pena to Tuva. The film Genghis Blues (1999) follows their journey.
artiest/kongar-ol-ondar.listen: Listen to Alash Hem and find the two layers in a single voice: a low droning tone and above it a whistling melody.

artiest/konrad-ruhland.text:
Konrad Ruhland was a German musicologist and choral conductor, born in 1932 in Landau an der Isar and died in 2010. He studied history, medieval Latin, theology and the history of the liturgy. That broad background gave him the knowledge not only to play early music, but also to understand it.

In 1956 he founded the Capella Antiqua München in Munich with a group of enthusiastic students. That group was one of the first to want to bring early Baroque and Renaissance music back to life with a scholarly approach. Under his direction recordings appeared of Gregorian chant, medieval hymns and motets, early Italian madrigals and a recording of Carmina Burana after thirteenth-century manuscripts. Christmas music from the fourteenth century was part of it too.

Ruhland passed on his knowledge until his death in courses, music weeks and summer schools, including at the University of Pennsylvania. He was also a sought-after choral conductor. His work shows how early music in the twentieth century acquired a sound of its own again: not a romantically exaggerated choral sound, but singing built up as far as possible from the sources.
artiest/konrad-ruhland.listen: Listen to a Gregorian chant from his recordings and notice the single-voice melody without accompaniment, which only follows the line of the text.

artiest/kool-en-the-gang.text:
Kool & the Gang is an American R&B, soul and funk band from Jersey City in New Jersey. In 1964 seven school friends decided to play together as an instrumental jazz and soul group under the name Jazziacs. The brothers Robert Kool Bell on bass and Ronald Bell on keyboards formed the core. The Bells grew up in a house in New York where Thelonious Monk also lived, who became Robert's godfather. After several name changes it became Kool & the Gang, and in 1969 the first album appeared on De-Lite Records.

The first big success came with Wild and Peaceful in 1973, with the singles Jungle Boogie and Hollywood Swinging. A declining period followed, until the collaboration with the Brazilian producer Eumir Deodato and the arrival of singer James J.T. Taylor brought a second peak between 1979 and 1986. Ladies' Night came in 1979, then Celebration in 1980, Get Down on It, Joanna, Misled and Cherish. Emergency from 1984 became the best-selling album.

The music developed from jazzy funk with a strong horn section into disco and smooth pop, always with a danceable rhythm. The group showed how funk and pop could flow into one another, and its songs were and still are played at parties. In 2024 came induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/kool-en-the-gang.listen: Listen to Celebration and notice the rhythm and the horns: the song is built for clapping along and dancing, and you can hear that in the very first bars.

artiest/kool-herc.text:
Kool Herc's real name is Clive Campbell, and he was born on 16 April 1955 in Kingston, Jamaica. As a child he heard the sound systems at neighbourhood parties there and the DJs who talked over the music, so-called toasting. In 1967 the family moved to the Bronx in New York, to an apartment building at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue. At school friends called him Hercules because of his height and build, and as a member of a graffiti crew he took the name Kool Herc.

In August 1973 he organised a party with his sister Cindy in the recreation room of that apartment building. That party is often regarded as the beginning of hip hop. Herc played hard funk records, such as those by James Brown, and noticed that the dancers loved the break most of all: the short section in which mainly the drums can be heard. With two copies of the same record on two turntables he switched back and forth, so that those few seconds grew into rhythms lasting minutes. His announcements and encouragements through the microphone were a forerunner of rapping.

He called the dancers b-boys and b-girls, words that are still used for breakdancers. Afrika Bambaataa and Grandmaster Flash quickly adopted his way of spinning and built on it. Unlike them, Herc did not make records himself in the first years of hip hop. He is therefore remembered mainly as the man who laid the foundation. In 2023 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/kool-herc.listen: Listen to Give It Up or Turnit a Loose by James Brown, a record that Kool Herc played at his first parties. Notice the sections where mainly drums and percussion sound: breaks like these were stretched by Herc with two records into a long, continuous rhythm.

artiest/korn.text:
Korn is an American band from Bakersfield in California. The group came out of the band L.A.P.D., of which James Shaffer, Reginald Arvizu and David Silveria were members. Together with guitarist Brian Welch and singer Jonathan Davis they formed Korn. The band writes its name with a reversed R, copied from the logo of Toys R Us, where some members had previously worked. A demo from 1993 was distributed free to record companies and fans.

The debut album Korn appeared in October 1994, recorded with producer Ross Robinson, and contains Blind. Commercial success came with Life Is Peachy in 1996, and above all with Follow the Leader in 1998 and Issues in 1999, which both debuted at number one on the American Billboard 200. Videos such as Got the Life and Freak on a Leash were shown a great deal on MTV. Later came Untouchables in 2002 and Requiem in 2022, among others.

The music combines metal and rock with hip hop influences, groove and dissonance, with lyrics about pain and alienation. Korn is regarded as a pioneer of nu metal. The debut album is seen as the beginning of that style and inspired bands such as Slipknot, Coal Chamber and Limp Bizkit. In this way the group stands at the beginning of one of the defining rock movements of the 1990s.
artiest/korn.listen: Listen to Blind and notice the interplay of the low-tuned guitars with Jonathan Davis's vocals. Hear how his voice alternates between whispering, talking and screaming.

artiest/kraftwerk.text:
Kraftwerk was founded in Düsseldorf in 1970 by Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider. The group began in the experimental German scene that English journalists called krautrock, alongside bands such as Can and Neu!. Where the others still used guitars and drums, Kraftwerk switched to synthesizers, drum machines and the vocoder. In this way the group became one of the roots of almost all electronic pop music.

The breakthrough came with Autobahn (1974). The title track lasts almost 23 minutes and describes a drive along the German motorway, with a Minimoog, electronic rhythms and sounds of engines and tyres. A shortened version of about three and a half minutes became an international hit. Trans-Europe Express (1977), with a rhythm like train wheels on the rails, Die Mensch-Maschine (1978) and Computerwelt (1981) followed. Kraftwerk worked in a studio of its own in Düsseldorf, Kling Klang, and presented itself as a machine: silent behind the equipment, later replaced by robot dummies. Wolfgang Flür and Karl Bartos played the electronic drums. Schneider left in 2008 and died in 2020; Hütter still leads the group.

The influence ran via New York and Detroit. Afrika Bambaataa played Kraftwerk at his parties in the Bronx and in Planet Rock (1982) used the melody of Trans-Europe Express. The techno pioneers of Detroit heard the group on the radio. In London the New Romantics danced to Kraftwerk, and synth-pop by OMD and Gary Numan built on their sound. David Bowie honoured Schneider with the track V-2 Schneider. In 2021 the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/kraftwerk.listen: In Numbers a computer voice counts: first in German, then in other languages. The voices came partly from an electronic translation gadget by Texas Instruments. Notice how the dry, tight electronic rhythms carry the numbers; hip hop and electro producers took over precisely that rhythm.

artiest/kronos-quartet.text:
The Kronos Quartet is an American string quartet from San Francisco. Violinist David Harrington founded the group in Seattle, where it first performed in November 1973. Since 1978 San Francisco has been its home base. The name refers to the Greek god Chronos, the personification of time. The line-up changed over the years, with Harrington as the constant force. The longest-lasting line-up, from 1978 to 1999, consisted of Harrington and John Sherba on violin, Hank Dutt on viola and Joan Jeanrenaud on cello.

What makes Kronos special is its repertoire. More than a thousand works have been written for the quartet, often on commission, by composers such as John Adams, Arvo Pärt, Philip Glass, Steve Reich, Terry Riley, Henryk Górecki and Kaija Saariaho. In addition, the group plays music from all points of the compass, from Azerbaijan and Afghanistan to Egypt and Argentina. The records let you hear that breadth: Monk Suite with music by Thelonious Monk, Music of Bill Evans, a record with work by Jimi Hendrix among others, and Different Trains with Steve Reich's Electric Counterpoint.

Kronos has recorded more than seventy-five albums and is sometimes called the best-known new music group in the world. In 2003 the quartet started the Under 30 Project, through which young composers under thirty receive a commission. The quartet showed that a string quartet does not have to stay in the classical concert hall, but can take part in popular culture and in music from all over the world.
artiest/kronos-quartet.listen: Listen to Different Trains and notice how the strings imitate the rhythms of trains and the rhythm of spoken sentences, so that a quartet sounds almost like a machine.
